meta.title: Bulgarian B1 Intermediate
meta.subtitle: 1000 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Bulgarian → English (see the Bulgarian, recall the meaning) and English → Bulgarian (see an English meaning, recall the Bulgarian). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1000 words for an intermediate learner, aligned to B1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand the main points of clear standard input on familiar matters regularly encountered in work, school, leisure, etc.' — a learner here is able to deal with most situations likely to arise whilst travelling, to produce simple connected text on topics which are familiar or of personal interest, and to describe experiences and events, dreams, hopes and ambitions and briefly give reasons and explanations for opinions and plans. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no graded Bulgarian word list is published that a deck could take whole, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 267 of the 1000 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — work and a career, education and learning, the media and technology, the environment, society and politics, law and crime, money and banking, health and a way of life, relationships and feelings, culture and the arts, the problems of travel, giving an opinion and arguing it, describing people and things, and the verbs of deciding, changing, comparing and making — and the other 733 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Bulgarian, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word, every form of a noun or a verb added together. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Every headword is printed in Cyrillic with its stress marked (кни́га, чета́), because Bulgarian stress can fall on any syllable and move as the word changes (град, градове́), and nothing else shows it; there is no transliteration, and the Bulgarian Alphabet deck, the first in this collection, teaches the letters. A verb is given in its first person singular present, the form a Bulgarian dictionary lists (чета́ 'I read', glossed 'to read'), since Bulgarian has no infinitive. The 525 nouns show their gender, their definite form (Bulgarian puts 'the' on the end of the word: кни́гата), their plural and, where it differs, the form used after a number; the 235 verbs show their aspect, imperfective or perfective, with the other verb of the pair beside them, their ти form and their past; and behind the All forms fold every noun's forms and every verb's present, past tenses and imperative by person, with the personal pronouns' full and short forms. Real example sentences come with 819 of the 1000 words, three apiece for 524 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, gender, aspect, stress and forms: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.

То възприема себе си, своите мисли и чувства като нещо отделено от останалото - един вид оптическа илюзия за неговото съзнание. Тази илюзия е своеобразен затвор за нас, ограничавайки ни в рамките на нашите лични желания и привързаността към най-близките ни хора. A human being is part of the whole, called by us Universe, a part limited in time and space. He experiences himself, his thoughts and feelings as something separated from the rest — a kind of optical delusion of his consciousness. This delusion is a kind of prison for us, restricting us to our personal desires and to affection for a few persons nearest to us. Our task must be to free ourselves from this prison by widening our circle of compassion to embrace all living creatures and the whole of nature in its beauty.
